p.src: Now Cao Pi, hearing that Cao Zhang was approaching at the head of an army, anxiously questioned his officers; one man stepped forward and offered to go and bring him to submission. They looked and saw that it was Jia Kui, Grand Master of Remonstrance. Cao Pi was delighted and immediately ordered Jia Kui to go. Jia Kui accepted the command, left the city, and went to meet Cao Zhang. Cao Zhang asked, “Where are the late king’s seal and ribbon?” Jia Kui answered sternly, “A family has its eldest son, and a state its heir apparent. The late king’s seal and ribbon are not matters Your Lordship should inquire into.” Cao Zhang fell silent, and entered the city together with Jia Kui. When they reached the palace gate, Jia Kui asked, “Has Your Lordship come to attend the funeral, or to contend for the succession?” Cao Zhang replied, “I have come for the funeral and harbor no other intent.” Jia Kui said, “If you harbor no other intent, why have you brought troops into the city?” Cao Zhang at once ordered his attendants and officers to withdraw, then entered alone and paid homage to Cao Pi. The two brothers embraced and wept bitterly. Cao Zhang handed all the troops under his command over to Cao Pi. Cao Pi ordered him to return and guard his fief at Yanling; Cao Zhang bowed farewell and departed.

p.src: Thus Cao Pi securely occupied the royal throne and changed the twenty-fifth year of Jian’an to the first year of Yankang. He appointed Jia Xu Grand Commandant, Hua Xin Chancellor of State, and Wang Lang Censor-in-Chief. Officials high and low were all promoted and rewarded. Cao Cao was posthumously titled King Wu and buried at the High Mound in Ye Commandery. Yu Jin was ordered to oversee the work at the tomb. Obeying the order, Yu Jin went there and saw upon a whitewashed wall of the tomb chamber a painting of Guan Yunchang drowning the Seven Armies and capturing Yu Jin: Yunchang sat aloft in imposing dignity, Pang De stood wrathful and unyielding, while Yu Jin knelt prostrate on the ground, pitifully begging for his life. In truth, Cao Pi despised Yu Jin for failing to die loyally when defeated and captured, surrendering to the enemy, and later returning. He had therefore ordered the scene painted beforehand on the white wall of the tomb chamber and deliberately sent Yu Jin there to shame him. When Yu Jin saw the painting, shame and anger overwhelmed him. His indignation brought on an illness, and before long he died. A later poet lamented him in these words:

p.src: Now Hua Xin memorialized Cao Pi: “The Marquis of Yanling has handed over his troops and returned to his own fief; but Cao Zhi, Marquis of Linzi, and Cao Xiong, Marquis of Xiaohuai, have both failed to attend the funeral. They should be called to account.” Cao Pi agreed and immediately dispatched an envoy to each place to inquire into the offense. Within a day, the envoy to Xiaohuai returned and reported, “Cao Xiong, Marquis of Xiaohuai, hanged himself for fear of punishment.” Cao Pi ordered a lavish burial for him and posthumously raised him to Prince of Xiaohuai. Another day passed, and the envoy to Linzi returned and reported: “The Marquis of Linzi drinks himself insensible every day with the brothers Ding Yi and Ding Yi, behaving arrogantly and without courtesy; when he heard that the royal envoy had arrived, he remained seated and did not stir. Ding Yi cursed me, saying, ‘In former days the late king intended to make my lord his heir, but slanderous ministers thwarted him; now the king has scarcely been laid to rest, and already you call his own flesh and blood to account. Why?’ Ding Yi then said, ‘My lord’s intelligence surpasses all under Heaven; by rights he should have succeeded to the great position, yet he has not been enthroned. You court ministers—how can you be so blind to talent!’ The Marquis of Linzi then angrily ordered his guards to beat your servant out with their staves.”

p.src: Now Cao Pi’s mother, Lady Bian, was deeply grieved when she heard that Cao Xiong had hanged himself; then suddenly she heard that Cao Zhi had been captured and his followers, including Ding Yi, had already been killed, and she was greatly alarmed. She hurried from her hall and summoned Cao Pi to see her. Seeing his mother leave her hall, Cao Pi hastened forward and bowed before her. Lady Bian said to him through her tears, “Your brother Zhi has always been fond of wine, heedless, and unruly. Trusting too much in the talent within him, he has given himself free rein. Remember that you were born of the same mother, and spare his life. Then even when I descend to the Nine Springs, I shall be able to close my eyes in peace.” Cao Pi replied, “I too deeply cherish his talent. How could I bear to harm him? I intend only to curb his nature. Mother, do not worry.”

p.src: Lady Bian withdrew, shedding tears. Cao Pi left the side hall and summoned Cao Zhi to appear before him. Hua Xin asked, “Was that not the Empress Dowager urging Your Highness to spare Zijian?” Cao Pi said, “It was.” Hua Xin said, “Zijian possesses both talent and wisdom; he is no creature destined to remain within a pond. Unless he is removed early, he will surely become a future menace.” Cao Pi said, “I cannot defy my mother’s command.” Hua Xin said, “Everyone says that Zijian can open his mouth and produce a finished composition, but I have never fully believed it. My lord may summon him and put his talent to the test. If he fails, execute him; if he truly succeeds, demote him, thereby silencing all the literary men under Heaven.” Cao Pi followed his counsel. Presently Cao Zhi entered, prostrated himself in terror, and begged forgiveness. Cao Pi said, “Though in affection you and I are brothers, by duty we stand as ruler and subject. How dare you presume upon your talent and show contempt for propriety? While our late father lived, you constantly paraded your writings before others, and I have long suspected that you had someone else compose them for you. I now require you to compose a poem within seven paces. If you truly can, your life will be spared; if you cannot, you shall be punished with the utmost severity, and I shall show no mercy.” Cao Zhi said, “I beg you to name the subject.” At that time an ink painting hung in the hall, depicting two oxen fighting beneath an earthen wall, one of which had fallen into a well and died. p.src: After Cao Pi succeeded to power, he renewed all the laws and oppressed the Emperor of Han even more harshly than his father had. Spies soon carried the news to Chengdu. When the King of Hanzhong heard it, he was greatly alarmed and consulted his civil and military officers, saying, “Cao Cao is dead and Cao Pi has succeeded him. He oppresses the Emperor even more harshly than Cao Cao did. Sun Quan of the Southland has folded his hands and declared himself their subject. I intend first to attack the Southland and avenge Yunchang; then I shall march against the Central Plain and destroy the traitorous rebels.” Before he had finished, Liao Hua stepped from the ranks, knelt weeping upon the ground, and said, “Lord Guan and his son were murdered because of Liu Feng and Meng Da. I beg you to execute these two traitors.” Xuande was about to send men to arrest them. Kongming remonstrated, “You must not. For now, the matter should be handled gradually. If pressed, they will rebel. Promote both men to commandery governorships and transfer them separately away from their present posts. Then they may be arrested.”

p.src: Xuande followed his advice and sent an envoy to promote Liu Feng and dispatch him to guard Mianzhu. Now Peng Yang was very close to Meng Da. When he heard of this, he hurried home, wrote a letter, and sent a trusted man galloping to inform Meng Da. The messenger had only just passed through the southern gate when Ma Chao's patrolling troops seized him and brought him before Ma Chao. After questioning him and learning the truth, Ma Chao immediately went to see Peng Yang. Peng Yang welcomed him inside and offered him wine. After several rounds of wine, Ma Chao sounded him out, saying, “The King of Hanzhong once treated you most generously. Why has his favor lately grown so thin?” Peng Yang, heated by wine, cursed resentfully, “That senile old hide has lost all judgment! I shall certainly find a way to repay him!” Ma Chao probed further: “I too have long harbored resentment.” Peng Yang said, “Raise the troops under your own command and join with Meng Da as our support from without. I shall lead the troops of Shu as our response within. Then great things may be accomplished.” Ma Chao said, “Your words are entirely sound. We shall discuss it further tomorrow.” Ma Chao took leave of Peng Yang and immediately delivered the man and the letter to the King of Hanzhong, recounting the affair in detail. Xuande flew into a rage and at once ordered Peng Yang seized, imprisoned, and interrogated under torture. In prison Peng Yang repented, but it was too late. Xuande asked Kongming, “Peng Yang intended rebellion. How should he be dealt with?” Kongming replied, “Though Peng Yang is merely a reckless fellow, keeping him alive will in time surely breed disaster.” Xuande therefore granted Peng Yang death in prison.

What am I to do?” Shen Dan said, “I have a plan that will prevent the King of Hanzhong from harming you.” Meng Da was delighted and eagerly asked what the plan was. Shen Dan said, “My brother and I have long wished to defect to Wei; you may write a memorial taking leave of the King of Hanzhong, then go over to Cao Pi, King of Wei. He immediately wrote a memorial and entrusted it to the envoy; that very night he led more than fifty horsemen away to join Wei. p.src: When Xuande had finished reading, he cried in fury, “That wretch has betrayed me! How dare he mock me with fine phrases!” He was about to raise an army to seize him. Kongming said, “You may send Liu Feng to advance against him and let the two tigers fight each other; whether Liu Feng wins merit or suffers defeat, he will surely return to Chengdu. We may then remove him and be rid of both dangers.” Xuande agreed and sent an envoy to Mianzhu to convey his command to Liu Feng. Receiving the order, Liu Feng led his troops forth to capture Meng Da.

p.src: Meanwhile, Cao Pi was assembled with his civil and military officers to discuss affairs when a close attendant suddenly reported, “Meng Da, a general of Shu, has come to surrender.” Cao Pi summoned him and asked, “Have you perhaps come only to feign surrender?” Meng Da replied, “Because I failed to rescue Lord Guan from his peril, the King of Hanzhong wished to kill me. Fearing punishment, I have come to surrender, with no other intention.” Cao Pi was still not fully convinced when news suddenly came that Liu Feng was leading fifty thousand troops to seize Xiangyang and was challenging Meng Da alone to battle. Cao Pi said, “If your heart is truly loyal, go to Xiangyang and bring me Liu Feng's head. Only then shall I believe you.” Meng Da replied, “I shall explain the advantages and dangers to him. There will be no need to move the army, and Liu Feng too will come and surrender.” Cao Pi was delighted. He appointed Meng Da Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, General Who Establishes Martial Might, and Marquis of Pingyang Village, made him Administrator of Xincheng, and sent him to guard Xiangyang and Fancheng. Xiahou Shang and Xu Huang were already at Xiangyang, preparing to seize Shangyong and its neighboring districts. When Meng Da reached Xiangyang and had exchanged courtesies with the two generals, he learned that Liu Feng had encamped fifty li from the city. Meng Da immediately composed a letter and sent a man to carry it to the Shu camp to invite Liu Feng's surrender. Reading the letter, Liu Feng cried angrily, “This traitor ruined the bond between my uncle and me, then sowed discord between my father and me, making me a man disloyal and unfilial!” He tore the letter to pieces and beheaded the messenger. The next day he led his army forward and challenged the enemy to battle.

p.src: When Meng Da learned that Liu Feng had torn up his letter and killed his envoy, he flew into a rage and led his own troops out to meet him. The two battle lines formed opposite each other. Liu Feng reined in beneath his command banner, pointed his sword, and cursed, “Traitor who has betrayed his state, how dare you utter such wild words!” Meng Da replied, “Death is already upon you, yet still you cling blindly to your delusion!” Enraged, Liu Feng spurred his horse, swung his sword, and charged straight at Meng Da. Before three bouts had passed, Meng Da turned and fled. Liu Feng pursued the apparent rout for more than twenty li, when a great shout arose and the hidden troops poured out. Xiahou Shang attacked from the left, Xu Huang from the right, and Meng Da turned back to renew the fight: three armies assailed Liu Feng at once. Liu Feng suffered a crushing defeat and fled, racing through the night back toward Shangyong while the Wei troops pursued behind him. Liu Feng reached the foot of the walls and called for the gate to be opened, but a storm of arrows rained down from above. From the gate tower Shen Dan called, “I have already surrendered to Wei!” Liu Feng was furious and wished to attack the city, but the pursuing army was almost upon him. Unable to hold his ground, Liu Feng had no choice but to flee toward Fangling, only to find the walls already covered with the banners of Wei. Shen Yi waved a flag from the gate tower, and a body of troops emerged from behind the city, bearing a great banner inscribed: “Xu Huang, General of the Right.” Unable to withstand them, Liu Feng hastily fled toward Western Shu. Xu Huang pressed the advantage and pursued him. With only a little over a hundred horsemen left, Liu Feng reached Chengdu. He went before the King of Hanzhong, prostrated himself weeping, and reported all that had happened. Xuande cried angrily, “You wretched cur! How have you the face to come before me again?” Liu Feng said, “It was not that your son would not rescue his uncle in peril; I was prevented by Meng Da's counsel.” Xuande's anger mounted: “You eat another man's food and wear another man's clothes; you are no figure molded of earth or carved from wood! How could you let a slanderous traitor hold you back?” He ordered the attendants to drag Liu Feng out and behead him. After the King of Hanzhong had executed Liu Feng, he learned that Meng Da had tried to induce him to defect, and that Liu Feng had destroyed the letter and killed the envoy. He felt considerable remorse; grieving besides over Lord Guan, he fell ill and therefore kept his army at rest.

u.src: When Meng Da learned that Liu Feng had torn up his letter and killed his envoy, he flew into a rage and led his own troops out to meet him.

The two battle lines formed opposite each other. Liu Feng reined in beneath his command banner, pointed his sword, and cursed, “Traitor who has betrayed his state, how dare you utter such wild words!”
Meng Da replied, “Death is already upon you, yet still you cling blindly to your delusion!”
Enraged, Liu Feng spurred his horse, swung his sword, and charged straight at Meng Da.

ja: にじゅうよさとついげき
u.src: Before three bouts had passed, Meng Da turned and fled. Liu Feng pursued the apparent rout for more than twenty li, when a great shout arose and the hidden troops poured out.
Xiahou Shang attacked from the left, Xu Huang from the right, and Meng Da turned back to renew the fight: three armies assailed Liu Feng at once.
Liu Feng suffered a crushing defeat and fled, racing through the night back toward Shangyong while the Wei troops pursued behind him.
Liu Feng reached the foot of the walls and called for the gate to be opened, but a storm of arrows rained down from above.
From the gate tower Shen Dan called, “I have already surrendered to Wei!”
Liu Feng was furious and wished to attack the city, but the pursuing army was almost upon him.
Unable to hold his ground, Liu Feng had no choice but to flee toward Fangling, only to find the walls already covered with the banners of Wei.

p.src: Now Cao Pi, King of Wei, upon assuming the royal throne, promoted and rewarded all his civil and military officials; then, commanding three hundred thousand armored troops, he made a southern progress to Qiao County in the state of Pei and held a great sacrificial feast at his ancestral tombs. The elders of his native district raised dust as they thronged the road, presenting cups and offering wine in imitation of Emperor Gaozu of Han's return to Pei. When word came that the Grand General Xiahou Dun was gravely ill, Cao Pi immediately returned to Ye Commandery. By then Xiahou Dun had already died. Cao Pi donned mourning and buried him with lavish rites.

p.src: In the eighth month of that year, reports declared that a phoenix had descended in Shiyi County, a qilin had appeared in the city of Linzi, and a yellow dragon had manifested in Ye Commandery. Thereupon General of the Household Li Fu and Assistant Grand Astrologer Xu Zhi conferred: these many auspicious signs foretold that Wei should replace Han. The rites for receiving the abdication ought therefore to be prepared, and the Han emperor made to yield the realm to the King of Wei. Together with Hua Xin, Wang Lang, Xin Pi, Jia Xu, Liu Yi, Liu Ye, Chen Jiao, Chen Qun, Huan Jie, and more than forty other civil and military officials, they went straight into the inner palace and petitioned Emperor Xian of Han to abdicate in favor of Cao Pi, King of Wei.
